description: A comprehensive study of international banking regulations (Basel) designed to protect banks from financial shocks, along with the identification, classification, and resolution mechanisms for Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) in India.

sections.title: Introduction to BASEL Norms
sections.description: International banking regulations issued by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) to strengthen the global banking system. 'Basel' is a city in Switzerland where BIS is headquartered.

key_concepts.explanation: The primary global standard-setter for the prudential regulation of banks. Its primary objective is to enhance understanding of key supervisory issues and improve the quality of banking supervision worldwide, thereby ensuring financial stability.

Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) is a measurement of a bank's available capital expressed as a percentage of its risk-weighted credit exposures. It ensures that a bank has enough capital (Tier 1 and Tier 2) to absorb a reasonable amount of loss before becoming insolvent. (CAR = Total Capital / Risk-Weighted Assets).

sections.title: Evolution of Basel Frameworks
sections.description: The progressive development of capital measurement systems to mitigate various financial risks over time.

results: Basel I (1988): Focused almost entirely on 'Credit Risk'. It defined capital and the structure of risk weights, setting a minimum capital requirement of 8% of risk-weighted assets.

Basel II (2004): Introduced a rigorous three-pillar framework: 1. Minimum Capital Requirements, 2. Supervisory Review Process (regulatory response to the first pillar), and 3. Market Discipline (disclosure requirements).

Basel III (2010): Developed in response to the 2008 global financial crisis. It introduced the Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB), Countercyclical Capital Buffer, and strict liquidity norms like the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) to prevent liquidity crises.

sections.title: Non-Performing Assets (NPA)
sections.description: Loans or advances for which the principal or interest payment has remained overdue for a specific period, causing them to cease generating income for the bank.

key_concepts.explanation: For term loans, if the interest and/or installment of principal remains overdue for a period of more than 90 days, the loan is classified as an NPA. For agricultural loans, the default period is 2 crop seasons for short-duration crops and 1 crop season for long-duration crops.

Early warning signals introduced by the RBI to identify potential NPAs before they default completely. They are categorized as SMA-0 (overdue for 1-30 days), SMA-1 (overdue for 31-60 days), and SMA-2 (overdue for 61-90 days). Upon crossing 90 days, it officially becomes an NPA.

sections.title: Classification of NPAs
sections.description: The categorization of bad loans based on the duration for which the asset has remained non-performing, dictating the provisioning requirements set by the RBI.

results: Sub-Standard Asset: An asset that has remained NPA for a period less than or equal to 12 months. The bank must make a standard provision of 15% on the outstanding amount.

Doubtful Asset: An asset that has remained in the sub-standard category for a period of 12 months (i.e., total overdue is more than 15 months). The bank must maintain significantly higher provisioning.

Loss Asset: An asset considered uncollectible and of such little value that its continuance as a bankable asset is not warranted. It has been identified as a loss by the bank, internal/external auditors, or RBI inspection, but has not yet been wholly written off.

sections.title: NPA Resolution and Management
sections.description: Legal and institutional frameworks established to expedite the recovery of bad loans and cleanse the balance sheets of commercial banks.

key_concepts.explanation: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act. It strongly empowers banks and financial institutions to seize and auction residential or commercial properties (collateral) to recover loans without requiring the intervention of a court.

A comprehensive, consolidated, and time-bound legal framework for resolving corporate bankruptcies. Its primary objective is to either restructure and save the corporate debtor or systematically liquidate its assets to pay off creditors.

National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) acts as India's premier 'Bad Bank'. It was established to aggregate and acquire large-value stressed assets (₹500 crores or more) from commercial banks, thereby cleaning their balance sheets and allowing them to focus entirely on fresh lending.
